title: A database copy dies at peak
summary: Black Friday traffic, and one of the database machines just disappeared.

statement.situation: Your shop's catalogue and checkout run against a database that has so far been a single machine. Traffic on peak days reaches 8,000 requests/s and about 90% are reads. Last year a machine failed at the worst moment: reads timed out, support was flooded with 'my order disappeared' reports, and the on-call engineer spent the evening deciding what to do.
symptoms: Latency climbs and requests time out when a database machine is lost
Some customers see old data after changing something
Recovery depended on someone noticing and acting by hand
requirements: Stay available through the loss of a database machine at peak
Writes (orders) must resume quickly if the machine holding them fails
Customers should rarely see stale data
constraints: Database machines are a fixed size: you can add more, not make them bigger
You decide how traffic reaches the database and what sits in front of it

background: Test your design under the peak with a lost machine. A second, unannounced test removes a different machine.
learningObjectives: Failover time and what it costs in write availability

references.title: PostgreSQL: high availability, load balancing, replication
AWS: Amazon RDS read replicas and Multi-AZ

scenarios.name: Peak with a lost replica
scenarios.description: 8,000 req/s for 3 minutes. A database machine is lost after one minute.

successCriteria.label: Requests succeed (≥ 98.5% over each run, counting the failover)
Writes recover within 40 s if the primary is lost

hints: After losing a machine, what's the load on each survivor?
A database that fails can be replaced automatically; how long does that take?
Reads don't all have to reach the database.
